name: The Hiawatha Playfield Red Oak

location.address: Hiawatha Playfield, 2700 California Ave SW, West Seattle

access: Free; Hiawatha Playfield is a public Seattle Parks playfield
transport: Not verified; city bus service on California Ave SW, exact stop and walk time not checked
story:
This oak is 55 feet wider than it is tall. When the tree expert Arthur Lee Jacobson measured it for a 2023 newspaper column, he found a crown 133 feet across on a tree 78 feet high, over a trunk 15 feet 8 inches round.

It is a northern red oak, a species from the other side of the continent, and it has spent its life at the edge of a playing field in West Seattle. Hiawatha Playfield opened in 1911, and the whole ground is now a city landmark. One local tree blog says this oak went in that year with the trees around it, when the Olmsted Brothers laid out what it calls Seattle's first playfield. That blog is the only source tying the tree to the opening, so read 1911 as likely rather than proven, which would make the oak a little over a century old.

The city lists it as a Heritage Tree, the programme Seattle runs with the group PlantAmnesty. Jacobson's verdict in 2023 was that it is not even halfway to the 250 years the species can live. Most trees on a list like this are admired for having survived. This one is still growing into itself, mostly sideways.

The pin marks the playfield rather than the trunk. Look toward the school side, and look for the crown first: it is the measurement you can see from a distance.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the crown, about 133 feet across on a tree only 78 feet tall, over a trunk 15 feet 8 inches round. It stands in Hiawatha Playfield, on the side toward West Seattle High School.

best_time.label: October, when that 133-foot crown turns red

name: The Chinese Scholar Tree of Cal Anderson Park

location.address: Cal Anderson Park, northwest corner near Capitol Hill Station entrance, Nagle Pl, Seattle

access: Free; public city park, open daylight hours; tree stands at the park edge beside the sidewalk and station entrance
transport: Capitol Hill Link light rail station is at the tree's corner of the park, about a 1 minute walk
story:
When the Capitol Hill light rail station was being dug, this tree stood just inside the construction wall, and a local reporter wrote in 2015 that it was probably only still standing because it was a Heritage Tree.

That listing, run by the city with the group PlantAmnesty, is the likeliest reason a century-old tree came through the dig. It is a Chinese scholar tree, also known as the Japanese pagoda tree, and the Capitol Hill Historical Society describes it as more than a century old and one of the trees still left from the Olmsted Brothers' design for the park. Nobody has published a planting year, so a century and a bit is as close as the sources go.

The same 2015 article called it the largest of its kind in the Pacific Northwest. No measurement has been published to go with that, so read it as a proud local claim rather than a ranking anybody has checked. If you have a tape measure, the trunk is the one figure this page is missing, and we would like it.

So the tree has seen the park as the Olmsteds planned it and the neighbourhood as it is now, with a train station built right beside it. The pin marks the corner rather than the trunk, but the corner does most of the work: come up out of the station entrance at the northwest of the park and it is right there.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by where it stands: the very northwest corner of Cal Anderson Park, beside the Capitol Hill light rail station entrance, at the edge of the pavement.

best_time.label: August, when it flowers cream while almost nothing else in the city does

name: The London Plane of Summit Place Triangle

location.address: Triangle of Belmont Ave E, Bellevue Pl E and Summit Ave E (nearest address 906 Summit Ave E), Seattle

access: Free; the tree stands in a small public street triangle (Summit Place Triangle), open at all times, on the pavement edge
transport: Roughly 10 to 12 minutes on foot from Capitol Hill Link station (about 1 km north-northwest along Broadway/E Roy St, walk time not measured precisely)
story:
This is a park where the tree is most of the park. Summit Place Triangle is the scrap of ground left where Belmont Avenue East, Bellevue Place East and Summit Avenue East meet, and a London plane fills it. In 2015 a Capitol Hill reporter described the effect rather than the trunk: it shades the entire space in summer, spreading 100 feet from side to side.

The city takes it seriously. It is an official Seattle Heritage Tree, one of the trees named by the programme the city runs with the group PlantAmnesty, and it is the closing stop on the city's own North Capitol Hill tree walk, which finishes at this triangle.

What nobody has written down is how old it is. There is no planting date, no girth and no height on record. It would be easy to borrow a date from the Olmsted plantings in Volunteer Park, a short walk away, and it would be wrong: that is a different story about different trees, and no source connects this one to it. A blank is more honest than a borrowed number.

So the page asks instead. If you live on Capitol Hill and know when this tree went in, or you pass with a tape measure, tell us and the figure goes here. It stands on public ground, open at all hours, about ten to twelve minutes' walk north of the Capitol Hill light rail station.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the crown, about 100 feet across, which shades the whole triangle. It stands where Belmont Ave E, Bellevue Pl E and Summit Ave E meet, near 906 Summit Ave E.

name: The Wedgwood Scarlet Oak

location.address: Northeast corner of NE 77th St and 38th Ave NE, Seattle

access: Free; stands in the public street right-of-way at the corner, viewable from the pavement. Do not enter adjoining private lots.
transport: Neighbourhood street in Wedgwood; bus service on 35th Ave NE about 3 blocks west, stop and walk time not verified
story:
This oak is held together with hardware rated to 54,000 pounds. A windstorm in March 2016 cracked its trunk, and instead of taking it down, Seattle's street-tree crews cabled and braced it, promised to inspect it every year, and estimated the work could buy ten years or more for what they called an otherwise healthy and vigorous tree.

That effort tells you its standing. It is a scarlet oak growing in the street right-of-way at a Wedgwood corner, which puts it in the city's own care, and it is one of the few such trees named a Seattle Heritage Tree and classed Best in City. It received its Heritage plaque at a ceremony in 2008. Arthur Lee Jacobson's Trees of Seattle counts it among the most outstanding of its kind in the city, and the local history blog that has followed it for years gives its height as 95 feet.

Who planted it is a neighbourhood argument rather than a record. The same blog thinks it likely went in during the 1920s, probably by the family who ran a plant nursery here, while an earlier post floated another family entirely. So call it roughly a century, give or take.

It has seen the corner change around it, most recently a new house going up beside it in 2020. Admire it from the pavement; the lots on either side are private. The pin marks the intersection, and the tree is on its northeast corner.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the cables and bracing in the crown, fitted after a 2016 storm cracked the trunk, on a tree about 95 feet tall. It stands on the northeast corner of NE 77th St and 38th Ave NE.

best_time.label: late October into November, when a scarlet oak earns its name

name: The Volunteer Park Copper Beech

location.address: Volunteer Park, behind the Seattle Asian Art Museum, 1400 E Prospect St

verified_sources: https://web.archive.org/ (CHS/McGarry 2015 via data/leads/seattle.json: largest in Seattle, 92 ft in 2000 per Jacobson)
access: Free; public Seattle Parks land, open daily
transport: Not verified; walk time from Capitol Hill not checked
story:
Two measurements taken nineteen years apart put this copper beech at almost exactly the same height: 92 feet when the tree expert Arthur Lee Jacobson recorded it in 2000, and 94 feet when the city surveyed it in 2019. Nineteen years, two feet: this beech was already near its full height when the century began.

The trunk is the bigger number. The city gives the trunk as 71 inches across at chest height, which comes to roughly 18 and a half feet round. A Capitol Hill writer, drawing on Jacobson's records in 2015, called it the largest copper beech in Seattle, and the city lists it as one of its Heritage Trees.

A copper beech is a purple-leaved form of the European beech, so this is an Old World tree grown up on the far side of North America. It stands in Volunteer Park, behind the building that houses the Seattle Asian Art Museum, a short walk from the park's giant sequoia. Its leaves open purple in spring and turn copper before they fall, which is where the name comes from.

What nobody has published is when it was planted. The city's measurements say what it has become and nothing about when it began. If you know, or know who would, tell us, because the age is the one number this page is missing.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the purple leaves on a tree 94 feet tall, over a trunk about 18 and a half feet round. It stands in Volunteer Park, behind the Seattle Asian Art Museum.

best_time.label: May, when the new leaves open purple

name: The Roanoke Street Lombardy Poplar

location.address: Roanoke Street Mini Park, E Roanoke St street-end at Fairview Ave E

access: Free; public mini park at a street-end on Lake Union
transport: Not verified; bus on Eastlake Ave E, stop and walk time not checked
story:
Lombardy poplars are famous for being narrow, and the city's figure for this one says otherwise: a trunk 81 inches across at chest height, which is about 21 feet round, under a tree recorded at 108 feet tall. For a tree planted almost everywhere as a slim green column along a fence line, that is an unusually heavy base.

It stands in Roanoke Street Mini Park, a scrap of public ground where East Roanoke Street runs out at Lake Union, in Eastlake. In 2010 the city named it a Heritage Tree together with three weeping willows beside it, and treated the four as a heritage grove, which is recorded on a plaque in the south part of the park. So the poplar shares the honour, and the shoreline, with three trees of a completely different shape: one shooting straight up, three hanging down.

The last city survey was in 2019, and naturalists logged the tree on iNaturalist as recently as April 2026. It is a different tree from the University of Washington's world's-fair poplar.

Nobody has published a planting date, and a trunk that thick on a poplar is worth a second look. If you pass with a tape measure, a girth taken at chest height would settle it, and the figure goes on this page.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the tall, upright poplar among three weeping willows, 108 feet high on a trunk about 21 feet round. It stands in Roanoke Street Mini Park, at the Lake Union end of E Roanoke St.

name: The Ballard Playground London Planes

location.address: Ballard Playground, near 2644 NW 60th St (register address), by 26th Ave NW

access: Free; Seattle Parks playground (OSM area Ballard Playground). Adjoins a school site: stay on the park side.
transport: Not verified
story:
Two London planes stand twenty metres apart at Ballard Playground, and the city measures them as near twins: trunks 76 and 75 inches across at chest height, each close to 20 feet round. Then they part company upward. One reaches 80 feet, the other stops at 64.

Both carry Seattle's Heritage Tree designation, and standing between them you see them as one sight: two trunks more than six feet thick, sharing a corner of a neighbourhood playground in Ballard. The city last surveyed them in 2019 and recorded both in good condition.

That survey is close to everything anyone has written down. No planting date has been published, no local history names them, and as far as we can find nobody has photographed them for any public collection. So the age is open, and so is the story: who planted a pair of planes this size beside a playground, and when. If you know, tell us.

The pin marks the larger tree, which sits inside the playground. Its partner stands a short way north, and we have not confirmed whether it is inside the park boundary or just beyond it. The playground borders a school site, so look from the park side and leave the school grounds alone.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise them as a matched pair of London planes about 20 metres apart, each trunk close to 20 feet round; the taller reaches 80 feet. They stand in Ballard Playground near 26th Ave NW.

name: The Seward Park Lake Washington Boulevard Douglas Fir

location.address: Seward Park, by Lake Washington Blvd S (register address 5898 Lake Washington Blvd S)

access: Free; inside Seward Park (OSM park area), public
transport: Not verified
story:
This is the Seward Park Douglas fir you can actually find. The city records it at 125 feet tall with a trunk 70 inches across at chest height, about 18 feet round, and it stands by Lake Washington Boulevard South rather than somewhere deep in the woods.

That matters because Seward Park already has a famous fir, and this is not it. The Big Tree, the 400 to 500 year old survivor of two forest fires, stands a little over a kilometre away in the old-growth interior, in a spot nobody publishes. This one is a city Heritage Tree with a pin that marks the trunk.

The last city survey of it was in 2019, and naturalists recorded it standing on iNaturalist in April 2026. Beyond that the record is thin. Nobody has published its age, and a Douglas fir this size could be a lot of things: a big tree is not automatically an old one, and we would rather leave the number blank than borrow one from its famous neighbour.

So stand at its base and look up 125 feet, then walk into the forest knowing the Big Tree in there is taller still. If you know when this one started, or what it has seen, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as a Douglas fir about 125 feet tall with a trunk around 18 feet round. It stands beside Lake Washington Blvd S (city address 5898), not in the forest interior.

story:
By the city's own estimate, this elm's crown is as wide as the tree is tall: 76 feet each way. It is a European white elm, Ulmus laevis, an unusual elm to find in Seattle, and the city lists it as a Heritage Tree.

Those numbers come from Seattle's street-tree inventory, which also gives the trunk as 50 inches across, about 13 feet round, and the height as roughly 23 metres. That inventory is the only source we have for this tree, the species included, and the pin on our map is the city's own coordinate for the trunk. A city crew last checked it in August 2019 and recorded it in service. We found no later sighting we could tie to this tree, so 2019 is the latest firm word on it.

Roanoke Park is a small neighbourhood park between Eastlake and Portage Bay, free and open from four in the morning until half past eleven at night. About 700 metres away on Roanoke Street stands a Heritage Lombardy poplar, which turns this into a short walk past two of the city's listed trees.

Nobody has published an age for this elm. If you know when it went in, or remember it as a smaller tree, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as an elm whose crown spreads about as wide as it is tall, some 76 feet, on a trunk around 13 feet round. It stands in Roanoke Park, at the city's register point for Heritage Tree TRE-100726.

story:
The trunk of this bigleaf maple is 63 inches across, about 16 and a half feet round, which puts it among the largest Heritage maples in Seattle's tree inventory. The same record gives it a height of 92 feet, about 28 metres, and a crown estimated at 99 feet wide. It spreads further than it climbs.

It stands in Ross Playground, a small Fremont park on 4th Avenue NW, free and open from six in the morning until ten at night. Bigleaf maple is the native maple of this coast, and the city has listed this one as a Heritage Tree.

Everything we know comes from that one place: the city's street-tree inventory, which also supplies the coordinate our pin uses, at the trunk. A city crew last checked the tree in August 2019 and recorded it in service. Naturalists have logged plants within 150 metres since then, as recently as September 2026, but none of those records is clearly this maple, so 2019 is the latest word on it we can stand behind.

Nobody has published an age for it either. A trunk this size invites a guess, and we would rather leave the line empty than make one. If you know how long this maple has stood over the playground, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its size: a bigleaf maple about 92 feet tall with a trunk some 16 feet round and a crown near 99 feet wide. It stands in Ross Playground on 4th Ave NW, at the city's register point.

story:
Pin oaks seldom grow a trunk this thick. This one measures 50 inches across, about 13 feet round, in Seattle's street-tree inventory, which lists it as a city Heritage Tree in Wallingford Playfield.

That inventory is the only source for it, and a thin one. It records no height and carries no notes, so we cannot tell you how tall the tree is. The pin on our map is the city's coordinate for the trunk. A city crew last confirmed it in service in September 2021. An iNaturalist record from August 2025 sits within range of the pin and may be this oak, or may be a neighbour; we cannot say which.

The record also fills in its planting field, but with a bookkeeping date rather than a planting, so it is no evidence of age, and we give none.

Wallingford Playfield is a neighbourhood park on Wallingford Avenue North, free and open from four in the morning until half past eleven at night. Pin oaks turn dark red to russet in autumn, which makes October and November the months to come and look for it.

Nobody has dated this oak or put a tape to its height. If you can do either, tell us, and we will put your figure on the page.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as an oak with a trunk about 13 feet round, 50 inches across, and in autumn by leaves turning dark red to russet. It stands in Wallingford Playfield, at the city's register point.

story:
Seattle realigned a street for this tree. At the corner of 16th Avenue East and East Aloha Street on Capitol Hill, the roadway, the curb and the sidewalk were all shifted to accommodate its size, as the Seattle tree expert Arthur Lee Jacobson recorded in his 2001 survey of the hill's special trees.

He listed it among the trees that are conspicuous and loved, rather than the big or the old. The city's figures suggest he was being modest. Its tree records give the trunk as 46 inches across, roughly 12 feet round, a height of 92 feet, about 28 metres, and a crown 69 feet wide. The tree is a city Heritage Tree, a listing the owner of the lot agreed to, and the city last recorded it in service in July 2024.

That lot is private, so this is a tree to see from the public sidewalk at the corner, and a crown 69 feet across leaves plenty to look at from there. Stay on the pavement.

A tulip tree is neither a tulip nor a poplar, despite the nickname tulip poplar. It is a magnolia relative, and its leaves give it away: four lobes, with the tip cut off square as if somebody took scissors to it.

Nobody has published when it was planted or how old it is. If you know the history of this corner, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its size, about 92 feet tall with a crown 69 feet wide, and by square-tipped, four-lobed leaves. It stands at the corner of 16th Ave E and E Aloha St, where the street and sidewalk were realigned around it.

story:
Seattle once realigned a Capitol Hill street to make room for a tulip tree. The one in Leschi Park is bigger: 106 feet tall to that tree's 92, and 52 inches across the trunk to its 46.

Those figures come from the city's tree records, which list it as a Heritage Tree on park land, about 32 metres high with a crown 74 feet wide. Across 52 inches of diameter, the trunk works out at roughly 13 and a half feet round, a little over four metres.

The records are also the only source for it, and they are not new. A city crew last noted the tree in service in August 2019. A naturalist photographed a plant close to the city's point for it in June 2026, but whether that picture shows this trunk is not certain, so treat the 2019 entry as the firm word on it. The pin sits at that city point inside the park; the crown itself has not been checked against it.

A tulip tree is a magnolia relative, not a poplar, whatever its old nickname says. Its leaves have four lobes and a tip cut off square, which is the quickest way to tell it from a maple.

Leschi Park is free and open from six in the morning until ten at night. Nobody has published an age for this tree. If you know when it was planted, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its height, about 106 feet, a trunk some 13 and a half feet round, and square-tipped, four-lobed leaves. It stands in Leschi Park, 201 Lakeside Ave S, near the city's register point.

story:
Seattle's tree records give this bigleaf maple a trunk 92 inches across, about 24 feet round. That is nearly half as wide again as the Ross Playground maple in Fremont, which the same records already place among the city's biggest Heritage maples.

The rest comes from the same entry: a height of 86 feet, about 26 metres, and a crown roughly 72 feet wide. Bigleaf maple is the native maple of this coast, and the city lists this one as a Heritage Tree. It grows on the private frontage of 1707 NW 62nd Street in Ballard, so this is a tree to see from the sidewalk, and a trunk that size does not need you any closer.

Everything here comes from one place, the city's tree inventory, which also supplies our pin. Nobody has checked that point against the crown, so treat it as the right block rather than the exact trunk, and let the address do the rest. A naturalist logged a plant within range in January 2023, but nobody has confirmed it was this maple, so the city's register is the firm word that it still stands.

It also starts a short Ballard walk. A Heritage giant sequoia stands about 300 metres away on NW 59th Street, a pair of Heritage Lombardy poplars a little further along that street, and the twin planes of Ballard Playground about 800 metres to the west.

Nobody has published its age. If you know when it went in, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, about 24 feet round, on a bigleaf maple 86 feet tall with a crown some 72 feet wide. It stands on the private frontage of 1707 NW 62nd St in Ballard; look from the sidewalk.

story:
Nobody has put a tape around the famous giant sequoia in Volunteer Park. This one, in a Ballard front yard, has been measured: 76 inches across the trunk, about 20 feet round.

The figures are the city's. Seattle's tree inventory lists it as a Heritage Tree on the private frontage of 1525 NW 59th Street, 95 feet tall, about 29 metres, with a crown only 47 feet wide. On those numbers it is a tall, narrow tree rather than a spreading one.

That inventory is the only source we have, and it also supplies the pin. Nobody has checked the point against the crown, so the address is the better guide. An iNaturalist observation from April 2026 falls within range of it; whether that record shows this sequoia has not been checked, so the register remains the firm word that the tree still stands.

Giant sequoias grow wild only in a narrow band of California's Sierra Nevada, so every one in Seattle was planted by somebody. Who planted this one, and when, nobody has written down.

The ground is private, so look from the sidewalk; at 95 feet there is no need to get closer. A Heritage bigleaf maple with a trunk 92 inches across stands about 300 metres to the north-west on NW 62nd Street, and a pair of Heritage poplars about 350 metres east along this same street.

If you know when this sequoia went in, tell us.

story:
Lombardy poplars are supposed to be slim, and these two are, in one direction only. The city records each crown at about 30 feet wide, on trees 122 and 121 feet tall.

They stand about ten metres apart on the private frontage of 1143 NW 59th Street in Ballard, both listed as Seattle Heritage Trees, and you see them together from the same stretch of sidewalk, which is why they share one entry here. The city's tree inventory gives the taller a trunk 77 inches across, about 20 feet round, and its neighbour 72 inches, about 19 feet. The Heritage poplar at Roanoke Street on Lake Union is recorded at 108 feet. Both of these are taller.

That inventory is our only source, for the measurements and for the pin, which marks the taller tree and has not been checked against the crowns. An iNaturalist record from June 2026 falls within range; whether it shows these poplars has not been checked, so the city register is the firm word that they stand.

The lot is private. Two columns this tall need no closer look than the sidewalk gives you. A Heritage giant sequoia stands about 350 metres west along the same street, and a Heritage bigleaf maple with a 92-inch trunk a little beyond it on NW 62nd Street, which makes three stops for one short Ballard walk.

Nobody has published when these poplars were planted. If you know, tell us.

story:
This sweet chestnut is far wider than it is tall. Seattle's tree records give it a crown about 69 feet across on a tree only 47 feet high, over a trunk 73 inches thick, about 19 feet round.

That is a low, broad tree on a very heavy base, and it grows on the private frontage of 502 North 47th Street in Fremont, where the city lists it as a Heritage Tree. Sweet chestnut is the chestnut of southern Europe, the one that ends up roasted.

The city's inventory is the only source we have, and it is candid. Besides the measurements, it marks a defect in the trunk and a problem in the roots, without saying what either is. It does record that the tree has not been topped. A Heritage listing is a mark of regard, not a certificate of health.

The pin is the city's point for the tree and has not been checked against the crown, so go by the address. A naturalist logged a plant within range in August 2023; nobody has confirmed it was this chestnut, so the register is the firm word that it stands.

The lot is private, so look from the sidewalk. The Heritage bigleaf maple in Ross Playground is about 800 metres away.

Nobody has published an age for this tree. If you know when it was planted, tell us.

story:
Coast redwoods grow wild in a strip of fog along the California and far southern Oregon coast. This one grows on a residential street in Wallingford, and Seattle counts it among its Heritage Trees.

The city's tree inventory gives it a trunk 62 inches across, about 16 feet round, a height of 85 feet, roughly 26 metres, and a crown 46 feet wide. It stands on the private frontage of 4625 Eastern Avenue North, so it is a tree for the sidewalk, and at 85 feet the sidewalk is a fine place to stand.

That inventory is the only source we have for it, the pin included. The point has not been checked against the crown, so let the address guide you. A naturalist logged a plant within range in May 2025; whether that was this redwood has not been checked, so the city register remains the firm word that it stands.

If you are unsure whether you are looking at a redwood or a giant sequoia, the other big Californian on this page, look at the foliage: a coast redwood carries flat needles in two neat rows, while a sequoia's are short, scale-like and pressed to the twig.

The Heritage pin oak in Wallingford Playfield is about 780 metres away. A thicker redwood, 98 inches across, stands on East Highland Drive on Capitol Hill.

Nobody has published when this one was planted. If you know, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as a coast redwood about 85 feet tall, with flat needles in two rows and a trunk some 16 feet round. It stands on the private frontage of 4625 Eastern Ave N in Wallingford; look from the sidewalk.

Few coast redwoods in Seattle's tree records come close to this one: a trunk 98 inches across, about 25 and a half feet round, on a tree 114 feet tall.

It stands on the private frontage of 2105 East Highland Drive, on the Capitol Hill side of Montlake, and the city lists it as a Heritage Tree. The same record gives a crown only 45 feet wide, a tall, narrow tree about 35 metres high.

East Highland Drive also runs past Volunteer Park, where a giant sequoia stands near the same street. This is a different tree and a different species, about 750 metres east of the park, and unlike the park's sequoia it has actually been measured. Coast redwood carries flat needles in two rows; the sequoia's are short and scale-like.

The city inventory is the only source we have, measurements and pin together. The point has not been checked against the crown, so go by the address. A naturalist logged a plant within range in July 2026; whether it shows this redwood has not been checked, so the register is the firm word that it stands.

The lot is private, so look from the sidewalk. Two more Heritage trees on private ground make this a short walk: the Aloha Street tulip tree, about 650 metres away, and a sugar maple on 17th Avenue East, about 750.

Nobody has published when this redwood was planted. If you know, tell us.

story:
Seward Park's Big Tree, the old-growth Douglas fir counted as the city's oldest, is around 150 feet tall. This giant sequoia in Madrona is 148, and it grows on the frontage of a house.

The figures come from Seattle's tree inventory, which lists it as a Heritage Tree at 1116 Newport Way, with a trunk 100 inches across, about 26 feet round, and a crown about 63 feet wide. The city last checked it in August 2023 and recorded it in service.

The record carries a three-letter comment, BIC. Seattle classes some of its Heritage Trees as Best in City, and that is the likeliest reading, but the register does not spell it out, so take it as probable rather than certain.

Giant sequoias grow wild only in a narrow band of California's Sierra Nevada, so somebody planted this one. Nobody has written down who or when. A tree of this height invites a guess at its age, and we would rather leave the line empty than fill it with one.

The inventory is the only source we have, and it supplies the pin, which has not been checked against the crown; go by the address. The ground is private, so look from the street.

The nearest other tree on this page is the Heritage tulip tree in Leschi Park, about 1.2 kilometres to the south. If you know this sequoia's story, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its height, about 148 feet, on a giant sequoia with a trunk some 26 feet round. It stands on the private frontage of 1116 Newport Way in Madrona; look from the street.

story:
This London plane is wider than it is tall: Seattle's tree records give it a crown about 89 feet across on a tree 77 feet high. And it does that on several trunks rather than one.

The city lists it as a Heritage Tree on the private frontage of 4123 12th Avenue NE, in the University District. That inventory is our only source, and it supplies the pin, which has not been checked against the crown. A naturalist logged a plant within range in August 2026; whether it shows this plane has not been checked, so the register is the firm word that it stands.

The lot is private, so look from the sidewalk. The University of Washington's world's-fair poplar is about 770 metres to the east.

story:
In May 2007 this sugar maple's trunk was 47 inches across. Seattle's tree records now give it as 58.

Both numbers sit in the same city entry. A comment there notes that the tree appears, with a photograph, in the book Trees of Seattle, measured at 47 inches on 17 May 2007; the current record gives 58 inches, about 15 feet round, and a height of 90 feet, about 27 metres, measured in June 2019. We have not seen the book itself, so both figures reach us through the city. Eleven inches is roughly three more feet of girth.

The tree is a Seattle Heritage Tree on the private frontage of 615 17th Avenue East, on Capitol Hill, and the city last checked it in July 2024 and recorded it in service. That inventory is our only source, pin included, and the point has not been checked against the crown, so go by the address.

Sugar maple is the maple of the eastern half of the continent, the one tapped for syrup, a long way from its home forests here.

The lot is private, so look from the sidewalk. The Aloha Street tulip tree, the one Seattle realigned a street for, stands about 230 metres away, which makes the two an easy pair, and a Heritage coast redwood on East Highland Drive is about 750 metres off.

Nobody has published when this maple was planted. If you know, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as a sugar maple about 90 feet tall with a trunk some 15 feet round. It stands on the private frontage of 615 17th Ave E on Capitol Hill, about 230 metres from the Aloha Street tulip tree; look from the sidewalk.
